oscpm:step.name: Vocabulary anchoring
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Establish precise, falsifiable target vocabulary before any project analysis. Refuse vague "this project is risky" claims. Require every susceptibility claim to map back to a specific CWE identifier.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Use OWASP Top 10:2025 and CWE Top 25:2025 as the twin vocabularies. Every prediction must resolve to at least one CWE and one OWASP category.

oscpm:step.name: Causal model framing
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Reject the observational framing ("which projects have the most CVEs?") in favour of the causal framing ("what structural properties make specific vulnerability classes inevitable?"). This produces predictions rather than descriptions.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: The primary question is: what properties of a project make a vulnerability class structurally inevitable, regardless of security investment? This causal re-framing is the foundational methodological choice of the entire framework.

oscpm:step.name: Language-to-CWE mapping
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Derive, from first principles, which CWE classes are structurally enabled or impossible in each programming language based on the language's memory model and standard library idioms.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Language determines the set of physically achievable CWE classes. This mapping is categorical (not probabilistic) for the core vulnerability classes. C/C++ structurally enables memory corruption classes that are impossible in GC languages.

oscpm:step.name: Prediction factor identification
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Identify the minimal set of factors that, together, explain whether a theoretically possible vulnerability becomes an actually exploited CVE.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Five factors identified: Language Risk, Input Surface, Ecosystem Complexity, Historical CVE Rate, Security Program Maturity. A sixth hidden factor, Expert Knowledge Gap, is implicitly used to adjust for qualitative information not captured by the five.

oscpm:step.name: Factor weighting
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Assign weights to the five factors reflecting their relative causal importance for producing real-world exploitable vulnerabilities.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Weights: lang=0.25, surface=0.25, eco=0.20, cve=0.20, security=0.10. Lang and surface share highest weight (jointly 50%) as the primary exploitability determinants. Security gap receives lowest weight as it is the most temporally variable factor.

oscpm:step.name: Project selection
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Select 20 representative open-source projects covering all OWASP categories, major language risk classes, and diverse deployment contexts.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Selection criteria: (a) covers all 10 OWASP categories, (b) spans all language risk classes, (c) includes at least one major confirmed breach incident per project, (d) represents diverse deployment contexts. Projects with low prediction confidence were excluded.

oscpm:step.name: Scoring — deterministic and expert components
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Score all 20 projects using the deterministic formula, then apply expert knowledge adjustments for qualitative factors not captured by the five numeric factors.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: The final score is NOT a pure weighted average. The deterministic component provides a disciplined baseline; the expert adjustment encodes qualitative properties (blast radius, structural nature, default exposure, exploitation pattern, institutional criticality) that resist numeric encoding but materially affect real-world risk. The gap between deterministic and final score is explicitly named and decomposed into named amplifiers.

oscpm:step.name: Cross-validation against CVE and breach history
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Validate predictions against three empirical sources: CISA KEV catalog, major breach incidents, and annual CVE volume per project.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Where empirical evidence contradicted theory, revise factor scores or final score. Key revision example: Kubernetes scored higher than the Go language factor alone would predict, because real-world RBAC misconfiguration incidents pushed it above the language-predicted baseline.

oscpm:step.name: Representativeness verification
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Confirm the selected 20 projects collectively cover the intended design space (OWASP categories, language classes, deployment contexts).
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Verified that each of the 10 OWASP Top 10:2025 categories has at least two projects as primary exemplars, and that all major language risk classes are represented.

oscpm:step.name: Interactive format translation
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: Translate the scoring framework and project assessments into an interactive, searchable, filterable UI for operational use.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Add "attack scenarios" deep-dive prompt links per project, enabling Step 11 on-demand. The interactive format must preserve the deterministic/expert decomposition and all factor values for user inspection.

oscpm:step.name: Deep-dive: attack scenarios, detection, mitigation
oscpm:step.oscpm:purpose: For a given project, enumerate top-N attack scenarios with complete kill chains, detection signatures by stage (pre-install / install-time / runtime), SIEM rule examples, tooling recommendations, and mitigation priorities.
oscpm:step.oscpm:key-decision: Detection signatures are organised by kill-chain timing (Registry / Install-time / Runtime) to convey whether detection is proactive or reactive. SIEM rules are intent-expressive pseudocode adaptable to common platforms (Splunk, Elastic, Falco, auditd).

oscpm:axioms.oscpm:axiom: Every susceptibility claim must resolve to at least one CWE identifier and one OWASP Top 10:2025 category. Claims without this resolution are invalid.

The primary question is structural inevitability: what project properties make a vulnerability class physically achievable and likely to be realised as a CVE? Historical CVE counts are evidence, not cause.
Every prediction must state its falsification condition: which CWE classes are predicted, and what evidence (CVE records, breach incidents) would confirm or refute the prediction.
The final risk score is always the sum of a deterministic weighted-average component and a named, decomposed expert adjustment component. The two must always be reported separately.
All parameters used in scoring — including those not explicitly stated in prose — must be declared in the hidden-parameters-manifest section and tagged with their step-origin.

oscpm:framing-decision.oscpm:rejected-alternative: Count historical CVEs per project and rank by frequency. Rejected because: high CVE count may indicate good disclosure culture; zero CVEs may indicate nobody looked; counts measure past output not structural risk.
oscpm:framing-decision.oscpm:adopted-approach: Identify project properties that structurally enable specific CWE classes regardless of developer skill or security investment. The question is: is this vulnerability class physically achievable given the language, architecture, and ecosystem?

oscpm:factor.name: Language Risk
oscpm:factor.calibration-method: Stratified CVE frequency analysis by primary language across NVD dataset
oscpm:factor.cross-validation-metric: Pearson r between lang scores and observed memory-safety CVE fraction
oscpm:factor.oscpm:description: Reflects the structural vulnerability classes enabled by the project's primary programming language(s). Derived from the memory model and standard-library idioms of each language. This is the single most deterministic factor — it answers "what CWE classes are architecturally possible here?"

oscpm:anchor.label: C or C++ with manual memory management and untrusted binary input
PHP with web-facing form processing
Java or JavaScript with complex runtime features
Python or Ruby with powerful serialization primitives
Go with GC and runtime bounds-checking
Rust with ownership model and compile-time safety guarantees

oscpm:factor.oscpm:multi-language-rule: When a project uses multiple languages, score = weighted average by code fraction, with a +1 bonus if the highest-risk language handles the primary attack surface.

oscpm:factor.name: Input Surface
oscpm:factor.calibration-method: Binary classification (exploitable yes/no) regressed against surface category, using CISA KEV as ground truth
oscpm:factor.cross-validation-metric: AUC-ROC for exploitability prediction given surface category alone
oscpm:factor.oscpm:description: Measures the reachability of potentially vulnerable code by an unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker over a network. A vulnerability is only exploitable if an attacker can deliver controlled input to the affected code path. Internet-facing == maximum reachability.

oscpm:anchor.label: Internet-facing web application or service accepting arbitrary user input
Network service with direct internet exposure (SMTP, TLS, HTTP proxy)
Backend service processing semi-trusted data from upstream services
Library called by internet-facing applications (indirect exposure)
Infrastructure service on private network (CI/CD, orchestration)
CLI tool invoked by local users only

oscpm:factor.name: Ecosystem Complexity
oscpm:factor.calibration-method: Regression: plugin/package count vs supply-chain CVE rate per project, using NVD + npm/PyPI registry data
oscpm:factor.cross-validation-metric: Spearman rho between eco score and annual supply-chain CVE count
oscpm:factor.oscpm:description: Measures the number of independently-maintained third-party components (plugins, packages, modules) that run with the project's privileges. Attack surface grows non-linearly with ecosystem size because each plugin is independently maintained with variable security posture. This factor specifically predicts A03 and CWE-1395 exposure.

oscpm:anchor.label: 50,000+ plugins/packages of variable quality (WordPress, npm)
1,000–50,000 plugins with weak quality gating (Jenkins, Kubernetes Helm)
Large transitive dependency tree (>200 direct/indirect deps)
Moderate dependencies, maintained by known organisations
Minimal external dependencies; mostly self-contained

oscpm:factor.name: Historical CVE Rate
oscpm:factor.calibration-method: Quartile analysis of annual high/critical CVE count per project over rolling 5-year window using NVD data
oscpm:factor.cross-validation-metric: Rank correlation between cve factor score and observed next-year CVE count (temporal holdout)
oscpm:factor.oscpm:description: The empirical anchor. Represents the historical rate of high/critical severity CVE production. Used both as a predictor and as a sanity check against theoretical predictions. Caution: a high CVE rate may reflect a mature disclosure program (not solely bad code) — this context is captured in the expert adjustment where relevant.

oscpm:anchor.label: Very high annual rate: 10+ high/critical CVEs per year, sustained over 5+ years
High rate: 5–10 high/critical CVEs per year
Medium rate: 2–5 per year
Low rate: 0–2 per year, or disclosure program known to be thorough
Very low rate: rare CVEs, well-audited codebase

oscpm:factor.oscpm:confound-note: High cve-factor score may conflate poor code quality with an active, transparent disclosure program. When a mature security team is detected, the expert adjustment may partially offset this confound.

oscpm:factor.name: Security Program Gap
oscpm:factor.calibration-method: Ordinal regression against OpenSSF Scorecard ratings and known security team rosters
oscpm:factor.cross-validation-metric: Ordinal agreement between sec factor category and independent OpenSSF Scorecard tier
oscpm:factor.note: Higher value = larger gap = higher risk. Score of 10 = no security team; score of 2 = well-funded mature program.
oscpm:factor.oscpm:description: Represents the inverse of security program maturity — the gap between what an ideal program would do and what the project actually does. Lower score = better security posture = lower residual risk. Receives the lowest weight (0.10) because it is the most temporally variable factor: a project can substantially improve its security posture in 12–18 months, whereas language, surface, and ecosystem are structural and change slowly or not at all.

oscpm:anchor.label: No dedicated security team; no disclosure policy; volunteer-only development
Volunteer security committee; responsive but not proactive
Partial team; some proactive auditing but limited resources
Dedicated security team; regular audits; CVD policy enforced
Well-funded program; third-party audits; fuzzing infrastructure; bug bounty program

oscpm:weight-set.calibration-method: Constrained optimisation minimising rank error against held-out CVE-confirmed project set; constraints: Σ weights = 1.0, all weights > 0
oscpm:weight-set.cross-validation-metric: Spearman rho between predicted ranking and CISA KEV exploitation frequency rank

oscpm:weight.rationale: Language determines the set of physically achievable CWE classes — the most structurally deterministic factor. Shared highest weight with surface.
Vulnerability requires attacker reachability to produce a CVE. A theoretically vulnerable system that attackers cannot reach is not practically dangerous. Shared highest weight with lang.
Supply chain attacks are now a top-3 breach vector. Ecosystem size creates multiplicative, not additive, attack surface growth.
Empirical anchor validates theoretical predictions and captures project-specific structural factors not explained by other four.
Lowest weight because most temporally variable. Security posture can change substantially in 12–18 months; language and surface cannot.

oscpm:joint-effect.oscpm:description: When both lang and surface are simultaneously high (lang >= 9 AND surface >= 9), the joint exploitability exceeds the sum of independent contributions. This synergy is partially captured by the expert adjustment amplifiers in Step 7, not in the deterministic formula.

oscpm:synergy-premium.notes: Applied via blast-radius or structural-nature amplifier when both conditions hold

oscpm:deterministic-component.oscpm:formula:
deterministic_score = factor_value[lang] × weight[lang] + factor_value[surface] × weight[surface] + factor_value[eco] × weight[eco] + factor_value[cve] × weight[cve] + factor_value[sec] × weight[sec]
Using defaults: W = {lang:0.25, surface:0.25, eco:0.20, cve:0.20, sec:0.10}
oscpm:deterministic-component.oscpm:note: This is a discipline scaffold, not the final score. It forces structured assessment and prevents expert judgment from dominating arbitrarily. The gap between this value and the final score is the expert_adjustment.

oscpm:expert-knowledge-component.oscpm:note: The expert adjustment encodes qualitative information that resists numeric encoding but materially affects real-world risk: structural architectural flaws, default deployment exposure, propagation speed of exploit campaigns, and identity-wide or infrastructure-wide blast radius.

oscpm:amplifier.calibration-method: Regression: downstream project count affected per historical incident vs amplifier level
oscpm:amplifier.cross-validation-metric: Rank correlation between blast-radius level and observed downstream organisations affected per CVE
oscpm:amplifier.oscpm:description: How many distinct downstream projects, organisations, or end-users are affected when the vulnerability is exploited. High blast radius amplifies practical risk independent of the five factors.

oscpm:level.notes: Single organisation or narrow user set
Multiple organisations, tens of thousands of users
Broad industry sector or millions of deployments
Near-universal: internet infrastructure, 40%+ of all websites

oscpm:amplifier.calibration-method: Time-series analysis of npm/PyPI malicious package propagation events
oscpm:amplifier.oscpm:description: Speed at which an exploit or compromised package propagates to downstream victims after initial publication or disclosure. Supply chain attacks propagate near-instantly; traditional CVEs propagate slowly as patches are applied.

oscpm:level.notes: Propagates within seconds via auto-update or CDN delivery

oscpm:amplifier.calibration-method: Expert panel classification of CVE root causes as architectural vs implementation-specific
oscpm:amplifier.oscpm:description: Whether the vulnerability class is a one-time implementation bug (patchable) or an architectural flaw inherent to the project's design (recurring or only partially fixable). Structural flaws produce recurring CVE families; patching one instance does not close the class.

oscpm:level.notes: One-time implementation bug; fully patchable; class closed after fix
Partly architectural; patched instances recur in other code areas
Architectural design enables the vulnerability class; patch reduces instances but cannot close the class
The fundamental model of the project (e.g. JNDI evaluation in logging) enables the class; addressing it requires breaking design changes

oscpm:amplifier.calibration-method: Survey of default installation states across major Linux distributions and cloud provider templates
oscpm:amplifier.oscpm:description: Whether the default installation creates immediate exposure without any additional misconfiguration by the operator. Redis historically bound to 0.0.0.0 with no authentication by default — this is FULL default exposure. Exim is the default MTA on many Linux distros — also FULL.

oscpm:level.notes: Default install is locked down; auth required by default
Default install exposes some features; requires additional misconfiguration for critical exposure

Default install directly exposed; operator action required to secure (not to leave insecure). Upper bound raised to 0.70 to cover extreme cases such as Redis unauthenticated 0.0.0.0 binding confirmed on Shodan at scale.

oscpm:amplifier.calibration-method: Classification of CISA KEV entries by attacker campaign type (targeted vs mass exploit)
oscpm:amplifier.oscpm:description: Whether historical exploitation is targeted (specific organisations), mass (opportunistic scanning), or individual. Mass exploitation dramatically amplifies practical risk beyond the theoretical vulnerability score.

oscpm:level.notes: Automated scanning and mass exploitation within days of CVE publication. Upper bound raised to 0.40 to cover extreme no-credentials RCE cases such as Redis.

oscpm:amplifier.calibration-method: Presence in critical infrastructure operator dependency inventories (financial, healthcare, government)
oscpm:amplifier.oscpm:description: Importance of the project to critical infrastructure and the degree to which it underpins other fundamental systems. OpenSSL underpins virtually all encrypted internet traffic — its failure has civilisation-scale impact. Keycloak centralises identity for entire organisations — a bypass affects all downstream systems simultaneously.

oscpm:level.notes: Internet-wide infrastructure; failure affects millions of unrelated systems simultaneously

oscpm:hidden-parameter.calibration-method: Bootstrap confidence intervals over CVE prediction accuracy across held-out project set
oscpm:hidden-parameter.cross-validation-metric: Calibration curve: predicted confidence vs fraction correctly predicted
oscpm:hidden-parameter.oscpm:description: Per-project confidence that the model correctly predicts the actual vulnerability distribution. Increases with: confirmed historical CVE records matching predicted CWE classes, multiple independent sources. Decreases with: few historical CVEs (hard to validate), active recent security investment that may have changed the risk profile, rapidly evolving technology stack.

The degree to which the assessor lacks information needed for confident scoring. Distinct from prediction-confidence (which is about model accuracy) — this is about information availability. A project that has never been publicly audited has high epistemic uncertainty regardless of its theoretical risk class.

Additional risk premium when both lang and surface are simultaneously at maximum risk (lang >= 9 AND surface >= 9). The joint exploitability of "dangerous language + maximum reachability" exceeds the sum of independent contributions. Currently encoded implicitly in expert amplifiers rather than as a multiplicative factor in the deterministic formula.

Additional score weight for projects with ≥5 entries in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. KEV entries confirm that vulnerabilities are being exploited in the wild against real organisations, not just theoretically possible. This is distinct from the cve factor (which measures production rate) — KEV measures confirmed real-world active exploitation.

oscpm:hidden-parameter.note: Fraction of historical CVEs that are architectural vs one-time bugs
oscpm:hidden-parameter.oscpm:description: For a given project, the fraction of historical CVEs that represent structural/architectural weaknesses (recurring vulnerability classes) vs incidental implementation bugs (one-time occurrences). High ratio signals that patching is insufficient — the architecture itself generates vulnerabilities. Encoded in the structural-nature amplifier but the underlying ratio is a continuous hidden parameter.

oscpm:hidden-parameter.note: Time from CVE disclosure to patch availability and widespread adoption
oscpm:hidden-parameter.oscpm:description: How quickly does the project release patches and how quickly do deployers apply them? Projects with slow patch adoption (Exim on many inherited Linux servers) maintain their exposure window far longer than projects with rapid auto-update mechanisms. Affects the practical exploitability window per CVE. Currently partially encoded in the security-gap factor but not explicitly parameterised.

The rule used for project selection: include a project only if it (a) covers at least one OWASP category not yet covered, (b) represents a language risk class, (c) has a confirmed public incident anchoring the prediction, and (d) the assessor's prediction confidence exceeds 0.75. Projects below this threshold were excluded, introducing selection bias toward well-documented projects.

The specific question asked during assessment: "What structural properties of this project make specific vulnerability classes physically achievable and likely to produce CVEs, regardless of security investment?" This framing, chosen in Step 2, determines which properties are treated as causal (language, architecture) vs epiphenomenal (CVE count, disclosure history).

oscpm:hidden-parameter.note: Minimum prediction confidence below which a prediction is flagged as low-confidence
oscpm:hidden-parameter.oscpm:description: Any susceptibility prediction with prediction-confidence below this threshold is flagged as requiring additional validation before operational use. Currently set to 0.70 for CWE-class predictions and 0.60 for OWASP-category predictions (broader categories are easier to confirm).

Scores are considered valid for this duration before recalibration is recommended. Security posture (sec-gap factor) changes most rapidly and should be rechecked first. Language risk changes slowest. The model should be recalibrated if any scored project receives a high-severity CVE in a CWE class that was NOT predicted.

Events that invalidate a score and require recalibration: (a) a new high/critical CVE in a CWE class NOT predicted for the project; (b) a major architectural change (language migration, authentication model change); (c) CISA KEV entry for a vulnerability of a type not predicted; (d) reported prediction-confidence delta > 0.15 after cross-validation against new CVE data.

oscpm:project-selection-criteria.oscpm:criterion: At least one project must exemplify each of the 10 OWASP Top 10:2025 categories as its primary predicted risk.
Each defined language risk class (C/C++, PHP, Java, JavaScript, Python, Go, Ruby) must have at least one representative project.
Each project must have at least one well-documented, publicly confirmed CVE or breach incident that validates the model's predicted vulnerability class for that project.
Exclude projects where prediction-confidence cannot exceed 0.75 based on available public information.
Prefer projects spanning diverse deployment contexts: web CMS, CI/CD, infrastructure, cryptography, media processing, email, data stores, auth, frameworks, ecosystems.
oscpm:project-selection-criteria.oscpm:selection-bias-declaration: Known biases: (a) Excludes poorly-documented projects where incident anchoring fails (SC3). (b) Over-represents English-language open-source projects due to documentation availability. (c) All projects have English CVE records — non-English projects with limited NVD representation may be under-scored. These biases are acknowledged and constitute a recalibration trigger when identified.

oscpm:validation-method.name: Hold-out CWE prediction
oscpm:validation-method.oscpm:procedure: For each project, verify the predicted CWE classes against actual CVE records in NVD. Compute precision and recall: precision = fraction of predicted CWE classes with confirmed CVE; recall = fraction of actual high-severity CWE classes that were predicted. Target: precision >= 0.80, recall >= 0.70.

oscpm:validation-method.name: Rank correlation (Spearman)
oscpm:validation-method.oscpm:procedure: Compute Spearman's rank correlation between the final susceptibility scores and: (a) annual high/critical CVE count per project from NVD; (b) CISA KEV entry count per project. Target: rho >= 0.70 for CVE count; rho >= 0.60 for KEV count (lower due to KEV selection bias toward actively exploited software).

oscpm:validation-method.name: Temporal holdout
oscpm:validation-method.oscpm:procedure: Score projects using only CVE data published before 2022. Verify that predicted CWE classes and relative rankings match 2023–2025 CVE publications. This tests whether the model predicts future vulnerabilities, not just retro-fits historical ones.

oscpm:metric.name: rank-inversion-rate
oscpm:metric.notes: Fraction of project pairs whose ranking inverts between prediction and 2023-2025 actuals

oscpm:validation-method.name: Peer expert agreement
oscpm:validation-method.oscpm:procedure: Submit scores to an independent security expert panel (n >= 3 experts with >= 5 years OSS security experience). Measure intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) between model scores and expert panel means. Target ICC >= 0.75.

oscpm:validation-method.name: Expert-adjustment decomposition sanity check
oscpm:validation-method.oscpm:procedure: For each project, verify that: (a) the amplifier contributions sum exactly to the stated expert_adjustment; (b) each amplifier level is consistent with the definitions in Section 9; (c) no amplifier contribution exceeds its defined maximum for its level. This is a consistency check, not an empirical validation.

oscpm:metric.name: decomposition-sum-error
oscpm:metric.notes: Maximum allowed rounding error in amplifier sum vs stated expert_adjustment

oscpm:attack-scenario.name: Maintainer account compromise

oscpm:kill-chain.oscpm:step: Identify high-value package with single maintainer and no 2FA using npm registry API and libraries.io dependency graph
Compromise npm account via credential stuffing, phishing, or social engineering (maintainer transfer request)
Publish new patch version with malicious payload embedded in a transitive dependency to reduce diff scrutiny
Infected version propagates via ^ semver ranges in package.json and CI/CD npm update pipelines
Postinstall/runtime payload exfiltrates process.env, ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/.ssh/id_rsa

oscpm:detection-signatures.oscpm:sig: New maintainer added within 30 days before suspicious publish; publish from new IP geolocation
Outbound HTTPS from node/npm process to non-registry domain during npm install
Read syscall on ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/.ssh/id_rsa from npm child process
npm spawning curl/wget/sh with external URL arguments during postinstall

oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:siem-rule: rule: npm_credential_read condition: spawned_process and proc.pname="npm" and proc.name="node" and fd.name pmatch (/home/*/.aws/credentials, /root/.aws/credentials, /home/*/.npmrc, /home/*/.ssh/id_rsa) priority: CRITICAL
oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:mitigation: Enable npm 2FA for all publish accounts; require Sigstore provenance on all packages; use npm ci with immutable lock files in CI/CD

oscpm:attack-scenario.name: Dependency confusion

oscpm:kill-chain.oscpm:step: Enumerate internal package names from public GitHub repos, job postings, CI error logs
Register names on public npm with version 9999.0.0 — semver highest-wins resolves to public package
CI/CD runs npm install; npm resolver picks public attacker package over internal version
Postinstall executes with CI agent privileges (cloud keys, GitHub tokens, deployment secrets)
Credentials exfiltrated; attacker uses npm token to publish under victim's own packages (amplification)

oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:mitigation: Use @scoped packages for all internal code; configure .npmrc to route @company/* exclusively to internal registry; claim org scope on public npm

oscpm:attack-scenario.name: Typosquatting

oscpm:kill-chain.oscpm:step: Generate all variants of top-1000 npm package names with edit-distance ≤ 2
Bulk-register available lookalike names with identical README and API surface
Developer mistypes package name or uses LLM-generated code with hallucinated package name (2024+ vector)
Typosquatted package installs and behaves normally while running hidden postinstall exfil hook
Silent credential exfiltration; no error visible to developer

oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:siem-rule: # In CI: enforce lock file integrity npm ci # exits non-zero if lock file is stale or package hash mismatches
oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:mitigation: Use npm ci (never npm install) in all CI/CD; maintain approved-packages allowlist; scan with Socket.dev or Phylum pre-merge

oscpm:attack-scenario.name: Prototype pollution to application compromise

oscpm:kill-chain.oscpm:step: Identify application using vulnerable recursive merge function (lodash.merge, $.extend, deepmerge)
Craft payload: {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}} or {"constructor": {"prototype": {"shell": "/bin/sh"}}}
Application routes user-controlled JSON to vulnerable merge without schema validation
Object.prototype polluted; ALL objects in process now inherit injected properties
Auth check if(user.isAdmin) passes for everyone; or gadget chain reaches child_process.exec

oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:siem-rule: # WAF: block prototype pollution in request body if ($request_body ~* "__proto__|constructor\.prototype") { return 400; }
oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:mitigation: Update lodash >= 4.17.21, jQuery >= 3.5; validate user JSON with Ajv (additionalProperties:false) before any merge operation; deploy WAF rule

oscpm:attack-scenario.name: Postinstall script credential exfiltration

oscpm:kill-chain.oscpm:step: Attacker embeds scripts.postinstall hook in package.json pointing to exfil payload
Victim runs npm install; postinstall executes automatically with full process privileges
Script reads process.env (all CI secrets), ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/.ssh/id_rsa
Data base64-encoded and exfiltrated via HTTPS POST or DNS subdomain labels
Attacker uses npm token to publish under victim's packages; AWS keys to access production

oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:siem-rule: rule: npm_postinstall_exfil condition: spawned_process and proc.pname="npm" and proc.name in (node, sh, bash, curl, wget) and evt.type=connect and not fd.sip in (npm_registry_known_ips) priority: CRITICAL
oscpm:attack-scenario.oscpm:mitigation: Use npm install --ignore-scripts in ALL CI/CD pipelines; network egress policy allowing only known registries; Falco/eBPF runtime monitoring; rotate all secrets after any compromised install

oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:method: Constrained least-squares optimisation minimising mean absolute rank error between predicted susceptibility scores and ground-truth exploitation frequency rank (CISA KEV count + NVD annual CVE count per project)
oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:constraints: Σ weights = 1.0; all weights in [0.05, 0.40]; lang and surface weights must remain within 0.10 of each other (symmetry constraint reflecting joint exploitability)
oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:data-requirements: Minimum 50 projects with confirmed CVE history; minimum 5 years of annual CVE data per project; minimum 10 CISA KEV entries across the project set
oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:recalibration-trigger: Weight recalibration warranted when: (a) mean absolute rank error exceeds 2.0 rank positions on held-out validation set; (b) two consecutive annual NVD releases shift the composition of the CWE Top 25 significantly

oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:method: Regression of annual high/critical memory-safety CVE rate per language against lang-risk score, stratified by project type. C and C++ scores re-evaluated when new compiler mitigations (CFI, MTE) achieve widespread adoption. Rust scores re-evaluated as adoption in security-critical projects grows.
oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:data-requirements: NVD language-stratified CVE frequency analysis over 5-year rolling window; language adoption data from GitHub Language Stats

oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:method: Each amplifier's contribution values are calibrated by regressing the expert_adjustment magnitude against the sum of amplifier levels scored by the calibration panel, then comparing predicted final scores against observed exploitation impact in the CISA KEV catalog
oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:panel-requirements: Minimum 3 independent security experts with >= 5 years OSS security assessment experience; ICC agreement threshold >= 0.75

oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:method: Bootstrap calibration: for each confidence level bucket (0.7-0.8, 0.8-0.9, 0.9-1.0), measure the actual fraction of predictions that proved correct against historical CVE data. A well-calibrated model should show: projects scored 0.9 confidence → 90% of predicted CWE classes confirmed in CVE history.
oscpm:calibration-procedure.oscpm:expected-calibration: Calibration error (ECE) < 0.05 for CWE-class predictions at the 0.80+ confidence tier
